extracted.intended_audience: industry regulated-entities, public interest commenters, and other participants in U.S. federal notice-and-comment rulemaking seeking post-Loper Bright comment strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting public comments on U.S. federal rulemakings after the Supreme Court's Loper Bright decision (which removed Chevron deference). Focuses on strengthening statutory-interpretation arguments and the administrative record to survive de novo judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with statutory text using interpretive canons
rubrics_metrics.description: Engages with statutory text using interpretive canons (textualism, purposivism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly analyze the statute's text and structure; apply recognized interpretive canons (textualist and purposivist approaches) to show why a particular reading is the best reading. Use concrete statutory citations and structural arguments rather than relying only on policy preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite legislative history when relevant
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislative history bears on statutory meaning, include appropriate excerpts (committee reports, floor statements, sponsor remarks) and explain their relevance. Use legislative history alongside textual and structural analysis to strengthen statutory-authority arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify statutory ambiguities and argue for the agency's or challenger's 'best reading'
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies statutory ambiguities the agency should resolve through best reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinpoint precisely where the text is ambiguous or silent and explain which interpretation is the 'best reading' (not merely 'reasonable'). For challengers, show why the agency's reading is wrong as a matter of statutory construction; for supporters, justify why the agency's reading is the best reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate the judicial-review framework (Skidmore-style persuasive authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipates judicial review framework (Skidmore deference factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare arguments that would persuade a reviewing court under a non-Chevron regime — e.g., emphasize the agency's thoroughness, consistency, expertise, and reasoning. Cite Skidmore-style persuasive authority arguments and structure comments to be persuasive on the merits to a judge exercising independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a factual record supporting policy choices independent of deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Builds factual record supporting policy choices independently of deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide fact-based evidence, studies, data, and examples that support the policy outcome on the merits so the record stands on its own even without deference. Fact-based comments remain essential for the policy record and to justify agency findings of fact and policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address Major Questions Doctrine considerations for significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses Major Questions Doctrine considerations for significant rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a rule implicates a major question (substantial economic or political significance), explain why the statute authorizes (or does not authorize) the agency action, and provide textual, structural, or historical support to counter or meet the Major Questions threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note congressional acquiescence or repudiation patterns where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes congressional acquiescence/repudiation patterns where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss patterns of congressional behavior (statutory amendments, funding decisions, oversight, inaction) that bear on whether Congress has acquiesced in or repudiated a particular agency interpretation. Use this evidence to support claims about statutory meaning or congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve statutory-interpretation arguments for potential appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should preserve statutory interpretation arguments for appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft comments so they clearly present and preserve legal arguments about statutory meaning and construction that could later be raised in litigation — include precise textual, structural, and historical claims in the administrative record rather than only in off-record advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how the administrative record supports de novo statutory review
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative record becomes the basis for de novo statutory review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that courts will look to the administrative record when exercising independent judgment; therefore, ensure the record contains the legal and factual materials necessary for judicial review (e.g., explanation of statutory interpretation, evidence, and reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish statutory-authority issues from policy-choice issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should distinguish statutory authority issues from policy choice issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate arguments about whether the agency has statutory authority from arguments about the wisdom or efficacy of the policy. Make clear which parts of the comment raise legal/statutory questions and which parts are policy objections or recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build the record showing an agency interpretation is wrong as a matter of statutory construction (for challengers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the record showing agency interpretation is wrong as a matter of statutory construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For regulated entities or challengers, compile textual, structural, historical, and precedent-based evidence in the record demonstrating why the agency's interpretation is incorrect. Explain statutory text and canons that undermine the agency's position and preserve those arguments for litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support the agency's best reading (for defenders of rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should support agency's 'best reading' not just 'reasonable reading' (public interest commenters defending rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending an agency rule, go beyond asserting reasonableness: marshal textual interpretation, statutory structure, legislative history, and interpretive canons to show the agency adopted the best interpretation. Explain why competing readings are inferior and document supporting evidence in the record.
